KEY MESSAGE 1...Periods of rain showers will impact the area
through much of the day, and lingering into tonight for Delmarva
and far southern New Jersey.

The cold front that crossed through our region Sunday night has
stalled well to our south across the Carolinas. Strengthening 
diffluence aloft, falling heights from an approaching trough,
and plenty of moisture will support periods of showers through 
much of the day, mainly south of I-78. Strengthening surface 
ridging to our north into the evening and overnight will allow 
some drier air to filter in, ending the chances of rain showers 
from the Philly metro and north. South of there, a few showers 
will remain possible overnight and into Wednesday morning. 
However, the main show for today's rain will be through midday
and wind down into the afternoon and evening hours.

Confidence is high that temperatures will be below normal 
starting today. Highs today will be mainly in the upper 50s and
60s, perhaps briefly reaching near 70 degrees for our southern
coastal areas near the warm ocean water. In fact, temperatures 
will likely struggle to get out of the 60s areawide through most
of this week. Lows will range from the mid 40s to 50s this week.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A strengthening surface low off the Eastern 
Seaboard during the middle and latter parts of this week will
keep persistent northeast to north flow in place through at
least Friday. Depending on the track of the low, it could bring
increased rainfall chances to the region Thursday night through
Saturday.

Confidence continues to increase that as a mid-level trough 
tracks eastward out of portions of the Midwest and Ohio Valley 
towards the Eastern Seaboard, surface cyclogenesis will occur 
off the coast of the Carolinas today into tonight. The initial 
track of the developing low is expected to be to the northeast, 
well offshore. However, with a strong high centered over 
portions of Quebec, a sharp pressure gradient over the region 
will at least lead to breezy conditions beginning today through
Thursday near the coast. The strongest pressure gradient, and 
thus winds, are forecast to occur on Wednesday into Wednesday 
night. It should remain mostly dry during the Wednesday through
Thursday period, though some showers may linger across Delmarva
Wednesday morning.

Given a consistent forecast for sustained winds 25-35 mph along
the Atlantic coasts of New Jersey and Delaware on Wednesday, we
have issued a Wind Advisory for the immediate coastal strip. The
advisory is in effect from 6 AM Wednesday through midnight
Wednesday night. Some gusts near 45 mph are also possible.

Friday and beyond, significant uncertainty remains. Models now 
fall into two relatively distinct camps, with one camp 
continuing to take the low northeast and away from the region. 
The other camp has the low deviating due northward or even 
northwestward to our region. The EC ensembles are generally 
clustered fairly tightly near the deterministic EC, which would 
favor this scenario. On the other hand, the deterministic GFS 
has the low continuing northeastward and the GEFS only has a few
members bringing the low towards the coast.

Unfortunately, the difference in sensible weather outcomes 
between these two scenarios is substantial. Should the low track
northeastward away from the region, any rain would be confined 
to the immediate coast, if any, and winds would decrease 
quicker. A track closer to the coast or even into the coast 
would lead to potentially significant impacts from rain and 
wind. For now, PoPs are maintained in the 20-40% range, and 
highest southeast of I-95. It is worth noting that there are 
several members in the ensemble suites which feature a middle 
ground scenario, where the low does deviate some but still 
remains fairly comfortably offshore. This scenario would lead to
some impacts from rain and wind, but the inland extent would be
fairly limited. We will continue to monitor trends closely as 
we try to nail down specific impacts and timing over the coming 
days. 


KEY MESSAGE 3...Multiple rounds of potentially significant 
tidal flooding expected for this week. The first batch of 
Coastal Flood headlines remain in effect with more likely to 
come.


With a slow moving coastal storm increasingly likely, the 
threat for tidal flooding has increased. Strong onshore flow 
that is projected to last for several days will result in water 
piling up across tidal tributaries and within back bays of 
coastal communities. Tidal levels will also be enhanced with 
astronomical tides increasing with the upcoming Full Moon on 
Saturday. This combination of factors will lead to widespread 
tidal flooding, some of which could get to the Moderate stage. 
While not currently forecast, the threat for major flooding is 
not off the table, especially getting near the full moon.
